explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Joel 2:18 says, “Then the LORD became jealous for His land, and He spared His people.” After all that locust trouble, that's a sentence worth reading twice. I'd read it a third time just to hear it.

Not this time, baker. The verse says the LORD “spared His people,” and scattering them isn't anywhere in it. The people had been weeping and praying, and what comes next is the LORD sparing them. I think that's a very good turn for a verse to take.

Close to a lot of Bible stories, but not this verse, friend. Joel 2:18 doesn't mention a test. It says the LORD became jealous for His land and “spared His people.” Sometimes the answer is simply the kind thing sitting right there in the text.

explanations.answer: Grain and new wine and oil
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. God says, “Behold, I will send you grain, new wine, and oil, and by them you will be satisfied.” Three things, and the verse says they'll bring satisfaction. If a batch of mine could promise that, I'd frame the recipe.

Shiny guess, friend, but that's not on the list. Joel 2:19 names grain, new wine and oil. Those are things you can eat and drink, and the verse says by them the people will be satisfied. Nothing in it mentions metal.

Good thinking, baker, but the verse doesn't send animals. God says, “I will send you grain, new wine, and oil.” Animals do show up in the very next verses, when the beasts of the field are told not to be afraid (Joel 2:22). But the promise in verse 19 is grain, new wine and oil.

True, baker. God says, “I will never again make you a reproach among the nations.” A reproach is something people look down on. Here God says He will not make His people that again, and I'd say that's one of the best promises in the whole passage.

It's actually True, friend. Joel 2:19 has God saying, “I will never again make you a reproach among the nations.” So the text doesn't say He'll keep making them a reproach. It says the opposite, and that's the good news.

Yes, baker. Joel 2:20 says the front ranks go “into the Eastern Sea, and its rear guard into the Western Sea.” One end of the army goes one way and the other end goes the other way. Nobody is left in the middle holding the map.

Fair guess, baker, since that's a sea people know. But Joel 2:20 doesn't use that name. It says the front ranks go into the Eastern Sea and the rear guard into the Western Sea. When the text gives you a direction, take the direction.

Nice try, friend, but the verse doesn't use that name either. Joel 2:20 sends the front ranks into the Eastern Sea and the rear guard into the Western Sea. So the blank is a compass direction, not a sea name. Easy to miss when you're stirring a lot of dough.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD has done great things
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Joel 2:21 says, “Do not be afraid, O land; rejoice and be glad, for the LORD has done great things.” The reason for the gladness is what He has done. I think that's a lot easier to rejoice over than a to-do list.

explanations.answer: Because the people have done great things
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend, the credit goes somewhere else. The verse says, “…for the LORD has done great things.” It doesn't say the people did anything great. The gladness is about what He has done.

explanations.answer: Because the enemy has begged for peace
explanations.explanation: That's a dramatic idea, baker, but the text doesn't say it. Joel 2:20 says God will drive the northern army away, and nothing there mentions begging. Then Joel 2:21 gives the reason for gladness: “for the LORD has done great things.”
Yes, baker. Joel 2:22 says, “for the open pastures have turned green.” Green pastures are a good reason for the beasts of the field to stop being afraid. Even a hungry animal can read that sign.

I see where your mind went, baker. But the verse says the pastures “have turned green,” not dusty. The change in the land is the reason the animals are told not to be afraid. Dust is out and green is in.

That's a creative one, friend, but silent isn't what the verse says. Joel 2:22 says, “for the open pastures have turned green.” It's a color, and it's the good kind. My oven can be silent. These pastures are green.

Not quite, baker. Joel 2:22 says the opposite: “…the fig tree and vine yield their best.” The trees bear their fruit and the vine isn't holding back. Nobody in that verse is saving their best for later.
Correct, it's False, baker. Joel 2:22 says, “…the fig tree and vine yield their best.” So they give their best, not hold it back. The trees bear their fruit too, and I'd say that's a happy orchard.

That's the one, baker. Joel 2:23 says, “He sends you showers, both autumn and spring rains, as before.” Both rains, and as before. A baker knows how much good timing matters, and I'd say rain on time is a gift.

Sturdy idea, friend, but a wall isn't in this verse. Joel 2:23 says the LORD has given them the autumn rains, and that He sends showers, “both autumn and spring rains, as before.” The gift here is rain, not bricks.

explanations.answer: A new king on the throne
explanations.explanation: Interesting guess, baker, but there's no king in this passage. The children of Zion are told to be glad because the LORD has given the autumn rains for their vindication. And He sends showers, “both autumn and spring rains, as before.”

Yes, baker, the first blank is full. Joel 2:24 says, “The threshing floors will be full of grain.” A threshing floor is where grain gets separated from the stalks. Picture it crowded with grain and you've got the verse.

Yes, baker, the second blank is overflow. The verse says, “…and the vats will overflow with new wine and oil.” That means more than enough, spilling over the edges. I know a mixing bowl that does this sometimes, and I do not enjoy cleaning that up.
That's the opposite of the verse, baker. Joel 2:24 says the threshing floors “will be full of grain.” After the locust years, full is the promise. Empty is the thing the promise is replacing.

Funny image, friend, but the verse doesn't go there. It says the vats “will overflow with new wine and oil.” Overflow means there's more than the vat can hold. That's a good thing to be short on space for.
Dry is the opposite of this verse, baker. Joel 2:24 says the vats “will overflow with new wine and oil.” Overflowing is as far from dry as a vat can get. The promise is about plenty.
That's right, baker. God says, “I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts.” He looks at the years that were lost and says repay. That's a promise to take in slowly.
Not quite, baker. The verse never says anything about forgetting. God says, “I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts.” The years are named, and He says He will repay them.

No, friend, it's the other direction. Joel 2:25 says, “I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts.” Nothing in the verse counts them against anyone. It's God promising to repay, and that's good news for the people.

explanations.answer: My great army that I sent
explanations.explanation: You caught it, baker. After the four kinds of locusts, God says, “…My great army that I sent against you.” He calls them His army, and He says He sent them. I'd read that line slowly, because it says a lot in a few words.

Not what the text says, baker. Joel 2:25 ends with “…My great army that I sent against you.” God is the one speaking, and He is the one who says He sent them. Enemies aren't named as the senders here.
That's not in the verse, friend. The text doesn't mention fathers or a curse here. God says, “…My great army that I sent against you.” Where the text stops, I stop too.
Yes, baker. Joel 2:26 says, “You will praise the name of the LORD your God, who has worked wonders for you.” With plenty to eat, praise follows. I'd say a full table can make a person thankful.

Not that one, baker. Joel 2:26 says the people “will praise the name of the LORD your God, who has worked wonders for you.” Praise is what the text says, so forgetting doesn't fit. He worked wonders, and they will praise.

I get why you'd wonder, friend, but doubt isn't in the verse. Joel 2:26 says, “You will praise the name of the LORD your God, who has worked wonders for you.” Wonders have been worked, and the people respond with praise.

explanations.answer: That God is present in Israel
explanations.explanation: That's the big finish, baker. Joel 2:27 says, “Then you will know that I am present in Israel and that I am the LORD your God, and there is no other.” After everything He does, this is what they'll know. I think that's better than any harvest.

explanations.answer: That the harvest will last forever
explanations.explanation: Good thought, baker, but the verse doesn't promise that. Joel 2:27 says, “Then you will know that I am present in Israel…” The thing they'll know is about God being present, not about the harvest.

explanations.answer: That the locusts will never return
explanations.explanation: Understandable guess, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. Joel 2:27 says, “Then you will know that I am present in Israel and that I am the LORD your God, and there is no other.” What they'll know is about Him.
True, baker. Joel 2:27 says, “…I am the LORD your God, and there is no other.” God says it plainly Himself. No fine print and no footnotes.

It's True, friend. Joel 2:27 has God saying, “…I am the LORD your God, and there is no other.” So the text does say it, and in His own words. I'd write that on the front of every cookie box if it fit.
